title: Statistical NLP: Models, Parsing and Information Retrieval
subtitle: Classify text with Naive Bayes and logistic regression, build word vectors from counts, tag with hidden Markov models, parse with probabilistic grammars, and rank documents with TF-IDF and BM25.
outcomes: Train and evaluate Naive Bayes and logistic regression text classifiers, implementing both from scratch
Build count-based word vectors with PPMI and SVD, and compare words with cosine similarity
Smooth n-gram language models and implement Viterbi decoding for hidden Markov model POS tagging
Parse sentences with probabilistic context-free grammars and the CKY algorithm
Build an inverted index and rank documents with TF-IDF and BM25
Evaluate statistical NLP models rigorously with precision, recall, F1, MAP and error analysis
prerequisites: NLP Foundations with Python and Corpora, or the same skills: Python, NLTK corpora, tokenisation and a bigram language model. Conditional probability, Bayes' rule and logarithms help (Statistics for Data Science and AI covers them), as does basic NumPy. You need Python 3.10 or later with NLTK, NumPy, SciPy and scikit-learn; the labs use small NLTK datasets, about 6 MB in all, and give the download commands.
description:
Before neural networks, the field learned to process language with probability and counting, and those methods still power search engines, baselines and many production systems. This course teaches them by building them. You'll write a Naive Bayes classifier from scratch and train logistic regression by gradient descent on cross-entropy, then represent words by the contexts they occur in, weighting co-occurrence counts with PPMI and compressing them with SVD into dense vectors.

Next come sequences and structure: smoothing n-gram language models properly, hidden Markov models for part-of-speech tagging with Viterbi decoding, and probabilistic context-free grammars parsed with the CKY algorithm and the inside algorithm. The last module builds the heart of a search engine: an inverted index, Boolean queries, ranking with TF-IDF and BM25, and the precision, recall and mean average precision that tell you whether it works. Every module has a lab on real data, such as the Penn Treebank sample, the Brown corpus and movie-review snippets, with exact expected output, and the capstone combines your tagger and a classifier to test, honestly, whether part-of-speech tags help tell opinion from fact. It builds on NLP Foundations with Python and Corpora and prepares you for Transformers and Large Language Models.

modules.title: Text classification
modules.summary: Classify documents with two classic models: Naive Bayes, which models how each class generates words, and logistic regression, which learns feature weights directly by minimising cross-entropy, and evaluate both properly.

lessons.title: Generative and discriminative classifiers
objectives: Explain the difference between generative and discriminative classifiers
Apply Bayes' rule to text classification
key_points: Text classification assigns a label to a whole document, such as positive or negative, spam or not, or a topic; it's supervised learning from labelled examples, with features extracted from the text.

A generative classifier models how each class produces documents, P(document | class), and the class prior P(class), then picks the class with the highest P(class) × P(document | class); Naive Bayes is one.
A discriminative classifier models P(class | document) directly, learning which features separate the classes without modelling how documents are generated; logistic regression is one.
Bayes' rule gives P(c | d) = P(d | c) P(c) / P(d), and because P(d) is the same for every class, the decision only needs P(d | c) P(c).

Generative models train fast and cope with little data, but their independence assumptions make them overconfident when features are correlated. A classic comparison (Ng and Jordan, 2001) found Naive Bayes often nears its best accuracy with fewer examples, while logistic regression reaches lower error with more data.

lessons.title: Multinomial Naive Bayes for text
objectives: Train a multinomial Naive Bayes classifier from word counts
Classify a document in log space with add-one smoothing
key_points: Naive Bayes represents a document as a bag of words and assumes that each word occurrence is independent of the others given the class, so P(document | c) is the product of P(word | c) over the document's words.

Training is counting: the prior P(c) is the share of training documents in class c, and with add-one smoothing P(w | c) = (count(w, c) + 1) / (total words in c + |V|), where V is the training vocabulary.
Without smoothing, a single word never seen in a class gives that class probability zero for any document containing it, whatever the other words say.
Classify in log space: choose the class with the highest log P(c) + Σ log P(w | c), skipping test words that aren't in the training vocabulary.
Binary multinomial Naive Bayes counts each word at most once per document, which often helps sentiment analysis, where whether a word occurs matters more than how often.

On NLTK's sentence_polarity movie snippets, a from-scratch multinomial Naive Bayes and scikit-learn's MultinomialNB(alpha=1.0) make identical predictions, 76.7% of them right, because they compute the same smoothed estimates.

lessons.title: Logistic regression: features, weights and the sigmoid
objectives: Represent a document as a feature vector for logistic regression
Turn a weighted sum into a probability with the sigmoid or softmax
key_points: Logistic regression computes a score z = w · x + b from a feature vector x, such as word counts, binary indicators, n-grams or counts of words from a sentiment lexicon, and learned weights w and bias b.
The sigmoid σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e^-z) turns the score into a probability between 0 and 1; predicting the positive class when σ(z) > 0.5 is the same as predicting it when z > 0.

Each weight says how strongly its feature pushes towards the positive class, so the largest positive and negative weights show what the model has learned, and features may overlap or correlate without breaking the model.
For more than two classes, multinomial logistic regression (softmax regression) keeps a weight vector per class and turns the scores into probabilities with softmax: exp(z_k) / Σ_j exp(z_j).

Regularisation keeps weights small to reduce overfitting: L2 adds the sum of squared weights to the loss and L1 the sum of their absolute values. In scikit-learn, C is the inverse of the regularisation strength, so a smaller C regularises more.

lessons.title: Training with cross-entropy, and evaluating classifiers
objectives: Explain the cross-entropy loss and its gradient
Train logistic regression with gradient descent
Evaluate a classifier with a confusion matrix, precision, recall and F1
key_points: Cross-entropy loss measures how well predicted probabilities match the labels: for one example L = -[y log ŷ + (1 - y) log(1 - ŷ)], which is small when the model gives the true class a high probability.

Its gradient with respect to the weights is (ŷ - y) x, the error times the features, so gradient descent repeatedly moves w by -η times the average of (ŷ - y) x over the training data, where η is the learning rate.

The loss is convex, so gradient descent with a suitable learning rate approaches the single best solution; stochastic and mini-batch gradient descent update from one example or a small batch at a time, which is faster on large data.

Starting from zero weights every prediction is 0.5 and the loss is ln 2 ≈ 0.6931. On the movie snippets, 300 steps of batch gradient descent bring it down to 0.5021, but scikit-learn's optimiser, run to convergence, reaches the higher test accuracy.

A confusion matrix counts predictions by true and predicted class. Precision is the share of predicted positives that are right, recall the share of true positives found and F1 their harmonic mean; with several classes, macro-averaging weights classes equally and micro-averaging weights examples.
Tune on a development set, touch the test set once, and read the misclassified examples: in sentiment data they're often negation, sarcasm or mixed opinions that a bag of words can't capture.

"""Naive Bayes from scratch, then logistic regression, on movie-review snippets.

First, once:  python -c "import nltk; nltk.download('sentence_polarity')"
"""

import math
import random
from collections import Counter

import numpy as np
from nltk.corpus import sentence_polarity
from scipy.special import expit
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix
from sklearn.naive_bayes import MultinomialNB


def load(seed=42):
    """(tokens, label) pairs, shuffled and split 80/20. The snippets are already tokenised and lowercased."""
    docs = [(sent, label) for label in ("neg", "pos") for sent in sentence_polarity.sents(categories=label)]
    random.Random(seed).shuffle(docs)
    cut = int(0.8 * len(docs))
    return docs[:cut], docs[cut:]


class NaiveBayes:
    """Multinomial Naive Bayes with add-alpha smoothing; binary=True counts each word once per document."""

    def __init__(self, alpha=1.0, binary=False):
        self.alpha, self.binary = alpha, binary

    def _words(self, tokens):
        return set(tokens) if self.binary else tokens

    def fit(self, docs):
        self.classes = sorted({label for _, label in docs})
        self.word_counts = {c: Counter() for c in self.classes}
        # TODO 1: count the words of each class (self._words(tokens) handles binary=True), then set
        #   self.vocab      every word seen in training
        #   self.log_prior  {class: log(share of training documents in that class)}
        #   self.total      {class: total word count of that class}
        return self

    def log_likelihood(self, word, c):
        # TODO 2: log((count(word, c) + alpha) / (total count of c + alpha * |V|))
        pass

    def predict(self, tokens):
        # TODO 3: for each class, log prior + the log likelihoods of the document's known words
        #         (ignore words not in self.vocab); return the class with the highest score
        pass


def accuracy(model, docs):
    return sum(model.predict(tokens) == label for tokens, label in docs) / len(docs)


def train_logistic_regression(X, y, lr=1.0, epochs=300, l2=1e-4):
    """Batch gradient descent on the mean cross-entropy loss (plus an L2 penalty)."""
    w, b = np.zeros(X.shape[1]), 0.0
    for epoch in range(epochs + 1):
        p = expit(X @ w + b)  # sigmoid
        if epoch % 100 == 0:
            eps = 1e-12
            loss = -np.mean(y * np.log(p + eps) + (1 - y) * np.log(1 - p + eps)) + l2 / 2 * w @ w
            print(f"  epoch {epoch}: loss {loss:.4f}")
        # TODO 4: error = p - y is the gradient of the loss with respect to z = Xw + b, so
        #         w moves by -lr * (X.T @ error / n + l2 * w) and b by -lr * mean(error)
        pass
    return w, b


def main():
    train, test = load()
    print(f"Train {len(train)}, test {len(test)}, positive share in test {sum(l == 'pos' for _, l in test) / len(test):.3f}")

    nb = NaiveBayes().fit(train)
    print(f"Our Naive Bayes: accuracy {accuracy(nb, test):.4f}, vocabulary {len(nb.vocab)}")
    nb_bin = NaiveBayes(binary=True).fit(train)
    print(f"Our binary Naive Bayes: accuracy {accuracy(nb_bin, test):.4f}")

    ratio = {w: nb.log_likelihood(w, "pos") - nb.log_likelihood(w, "neg")
             for w in nb.vocab if nb.word_counts["pos"][w] + nb.word_counts["neg"][w] >= 10}
    ranked = sorted(ratio, key=lambda w: (ratio[w], w))
    print("Most negative words:", ranked[:6])
    print("Most positive words:", ranked[-6:][::-1])

    vectoriser = CountVectorizer(analyzer=lambda tokens: tokens)  # the documents are token lists already
    X_train = vectoriser.fit_transform([t for t, _ in train])
    X_test = vectoriser.transform([t for t, _ in test])
    y_train = np.array([l == "pos" for _, l in train], dtype=float)
    y_test = np.array([l == "pos" for _, l in test], dtype=float)
    sk_nb = MultinomialNB(alpha=1.0).fit(X_train, y_train)
    print(f"scikit-learn MultinomialNB: accuracy {(sk_nb.predict(X_test) == y_test).mean():.4f}")

    print("Logistic regression by gradient descent:")
    w, b = train_logistic_regression(X_train, y_train)
    ours = ((X_test @ w + b) > 0).astype(float)
    print(f"Our logistic regression: accuracy {(ours == y_test).mean():.4f}")
    sk_lr = LogisticRegression(C=1.0, max_iter=1000).fit(X_train, y_train)
    pred = sk_lr.predict(X_test)
    print(f"scikit-learn LogisticRegression: accuracy {(pred == y_test).mean():.4f}")

    print("Confusion matrix (rows: true neg, pos):", confusion_matrix(y_test, pred).tolist())
    wrong = [" ".join(tokens) for (tokens, _), p, t in zip(test, pred, y_test) if p != t]
    print("First misclassified:", wrong[0])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

hints: self.total[c] is the sum of all the word counts in class c, not the number of distinct words.
If your accuracy differs slightly from scikit-learn's, check that unknown test words are skipped and that |V| is the size of the whole training vocabulary, not one class's.
Your logistic regression is less accurate than scikit-learn's because 300 steps of plain gradient descent haven't converged; try more epochs and watch the loss.

modules.title: Vector semantics and embeddings
modules.summary: Represent words by the company they keep: build term-document and word-context matrices, weight them with PPMI, compare words with cosine similarity, and compress the counts into dense vectors with SVD, the bridge to learned embeddings.

lessons.title: The distributional hypothesis and co-occurrence matrices
objectives: State the distributional hypothesis
Build term-document and word-context co-occurrence matrices
key_points: The distributional hypothesis says that words occurring in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings; the linguist J. R. Firth put it as 'You shall know a word by the company it keeps' (1957).

A term-document matrix has a row per word and a column per document, each cell counting the word in that document; documents are compared by their columns (the basis of the vector space model in search) and words by their rows.

A word-context matrix counts how often each context word appears within a window, such as ±2 words, around each target word; small windows capture close, often syntactic similarity and larger ones topical relatedness.

These matrices are sparse: with the 5,000 most frequent Brown corpus words as both rows and contexts and a ±2-word window, only 2.8% of the 25 million cells are non-zero, so they're stored in sparse formats such as SciPy's CSR.
Raw counts are dominated by frequent function words: nearly every noun co-occurs with 'the' and 'of', so raw-count vectors make words look alike for uninformative reasons.

lessons.title: Weighting with PMI and PPMI
objectives: Calculate pointwise mutual information from co-occurrence counts
Explain why PPMI and context smoothing are used
key_points: Pointwise mutual information compares how often a word and a context occur together with how often they would by chance: PMI(w, c) = log2(P(w, c) / (P(w) P(c))), with the probabilities estimated from the co-occurrence counts.

PMI is positive when a pair occurs more often than chance, zero at chance and negative when less often; negative values need enormous corpora to estimate reliably, so positive PMI (PPMI) replaces them with zero.

PMI is biased towards rare events: a rare context seen once with a rare word scores very high. Raising context counts to the power 0.75 before normalising them, or adding k to every count, reduces the bias.
Weighting changes the neighbours: in the Brown corpus, raw counts make 'wife' look closest to 'chest' and 'hat', while PPMI gives 'mother', 'husband' and 'daughter'.
TF-IDF is the corresponding weighting for term-document matrices: it favours words that are frequent in a document but rare across documents, as the information retrieval module shows.

steps.do: Compute PPMI for a small 3 x 3 count matrix with NumPy.
steps.code:
import numpy as np
M = np.array([[2, 0, 1], [0, 3, 1], [1, 1, 0]], dtype=float)
P = M / M.sum()
pw, pc = P.sum(1, keepdims=True), P.sum(0, keepdims=True)
with np.errstate(divide='ignore'):
    pmi = np.log2(P / (pw * pc))
np.round(np.maximum(pmi, 0), 3)
steps.see: [[1. 0. 0.585] [0. 0.755 0.17] [0.585 0.17 0.]]: zero counts give -inf, which PPMI turns into 0.

lessons.title: Cosine similarity and nearest neighbours
objectives: Compute cosine similarity between word vectors
Find and evaluate a word's nearest neighbours
key_points: The dot product of two vectors grows with their lengths, which favours frequent words; cosine similarity divides by both lengths, cos(a, b) = a · b / (|a| |b|), so it measures only the angle between them.
Cosine ranges from -1 to 1, and from 0 to 1 for non-negative vectors such as counts or PPMI; after normalising every row to length 1, one matrix product gives a word's cosine with every other word.
A word's nearest neighbours are the words with the highest cosine to it; they show what a representation has captured and are the usual first check of a vector space.
Count vectors capture second-order similarity: two words can be close without ever occurring together because they share contexts, as 'tuesday' and 'wednesday' do.

Vector spaces are evaluated intrinsically, by correlating their similarities with human ratings of word pairs (Spearman correlation on datasets such as WordSim-353 and SimLex-999), and extrinsically, by how much they help a downstream task.

lessons.title: Dense vectors from counts: SVD and latent semantic analysis
objectives: Reduce a sparse co-occurrence matrix to dense vectors with truncated SVD
Relate count-based vectors to learned word embeddings
key_points: Singular value decomposition factors a matrix M into U Σ V^T; keeping only the k largest singular values gives the best rank-k approximation of M in the least-squares sense.
Truncated SVD of a PPMI or TF-IDF matrix gives each word a dense vector of k numbers, typically 100 to 300; scikit-learn's TruncatedSVD works directly on sparse matrices.

Applied to term-document matrices for search, this is latent semantic analysis (LSA, also called latent semantic indexing): dimensions that blend related words let documents match queries that use synonyms.

Dense vectors generalise better than sparse ones because they smooth over contexts a word happened not to occur in: in the lab, 100 SVD dimensions of the Brown PPMI matrix make 'red' closest to 'white', 'black', 'yellow', 'blue' and 'pink'.

Predictive methods such as word2vec learn dense vectors directly, and its skip-gram with negative sampling has been shown to implicitly factorise a shifted PMI matrix (Levy and Goldberg, 2014), so count-based and predictive embeddings are close relatives.

"""Word vectors from co-occurrence counts in the Brown corpus: raw counts, PPMI and SVD.

First, once:  python -c "import nltk; nltk.download('brown')"
"""

from collections import Counter

import numpy as np
import scipy.sparse as sp
from nltk.corpus import brown
from sklearn.decomposition import TruncatedSVD
from sklearn.preprocessing import normalize

VOCAB_SIZE, WINDOW = 5000, 2
PROBES = ["week", "tuesday", "school", "wife", "red"]


def cooccurrence(sents, vocab, window=WINDOW):
    """A word-by-context count matrix: how often each context word is within `window` words, in the same sentence."""
    index = {w: i for i, w in enumerate(vocab)}
    rows, cols = [], []
    for sent in sents:
        ids = [index.get(w) for w in sent]  # None for words outside the vocabulary
        # TODO 1: for every position i with a vocabulary word, and every other position j at most `window`
        #         away in the same sentence that also holds a vocabulary word, append ids[i] to rows and ids[j] to cols
        pass
    n = len(vocab)
    return sp.coo_matrix((np.ones(len(rows)), (rows, cols)), shape=(n, n)).tocsr()  # duplicates are summed


def ppmi(counts, alpha=0.75):
    """Positive pointwise mutual information, with the context distribution raised to alpha (smoothing)."""
    total = counts.sum()
    p_word = np.asarray(counts.sum(axis=1)).ravel() / total
    context = np.asarray(counts.sum(axis=0)).ravel() ** alpha
    p_context = context / context.sum()
    m = counts.tocoo()  # m.row, m.col and m.data list the non-zero cells
    # TODO 2: pmi = log2(P(w, c) / (P(w) * P(c))) for each non-zero cell, with P(w, c) = m.data / total;
    #         keep only the positive values and return them as a csr_matrix of the same shape
    pass


def neighbours(matrix, vocab, word, k=5):
    unit = normalize(matrix)  # rows of length 1, so dot products are cosines
    i = vocab.index(word)
    sims = unit @ unit[i].T
    sims = np.asarray(sims.todense()).ravel() if sp.issparse(sims) else np.asarray(sims).ravel()
    sims[i] = -1  # leave the word itself out
    best = np.argsort(-sims, kind="stable")[:k]
    return [f"{vocab[j]} {sims[j]:.2f}" for j in best]


def main():
    sents = [[w.lower() for w in s if w.isalpha()] for s in brown.sents()]
    freq = Counter(w for s in sents for w in s)
    vocab = [w for w, _ in freq.most_common(VOCAB_SIZE)]
    counts = cooccurrence(sents, vocab)
    print(f"Matrix {counts.shape[0]} x {counts.shape[1]}, {counts.nnz} non-zero cells "
          f"({counts.nnz / counts.shape[0] ** 2:.1%} full), {int(counts.sum())} co-occurrences")

    weighted = ppmi(counts)
    print(f"PPMI keeps {weighted.nnz} positive cells")
    svd = TruncatedSVD(n_components=100, random_state=0)
    dense = svd.fit_transform(weighted)
    print(f"SVD: 100 dimensions explain {svd.explained_variance_ratio_.sum():.1%} of the variance")

    for word in PROBES:
        print(f"{word}")
        print("  counts:", neighbours(counts, vocab, word))
        print("  PPMI:  ", neighbours(weighted, vocab, word))
        print("  SVD:   ", neighbours(dense, vocab, word))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

hints: range(max(0, i - window), min(len(ids), i + window + 1)) covers the window around position i; skip j == i and positions holding None.
m.row and m.col index the non-zero cells, so p_word[m.row] and p_context[m.col] line up with m.data.
If PPMI keeps every cell, the logarithm or the smoothing is wrong: about one non-zero cell in six has a PMI of zero or less.

modules.title: Markov models and POS tagging
modules.summary: Model sequences with the Markov assumption: smooth n-gram language models properly, then build hidden Markov models for part-of-speech tagging, decode them with the Viterbi algorithm and handle words never seen in training.

lessons.title: N-gram language models and smoothing
objectives: State the Markov assumption behind n-gram models
Compare add-k, interpolation, backoff and Kneser-Ney smoothing
key_points: The Markov assumption approximates the probability of a word given its whole history by its probability given only the last n - 1 words: a bigram model uses one word of history and a trigram model two.
Maximum likelihood estimates give zero to every n-gram missing from the training data, and the higher n is, the more of any test text is unseen, so higher-order models need smoothing even more.

Add-one smoothing, met in NLP Foundations with Python and Corpora, moves too much probability to unseen events; add-k with a small k tuned on held-out data does better, but still treats every unseen word alike.

Interpolation mixes orders, P = λ3 P(w | u, v) + λ2 P(w | v) + λ1 P(w), with the λs summing to 1 and tuned on held-out data; backoff uses the highest order that has counts, and Katz backoff discounts it so the probabilities still sum to 1.

Kneser-Ney smoothing subtracts a fixed discount from each count and gives the freed probability to a continuation distribution, based on how many different words a word follows: 'Francisco' is frequent but follows almost only 'San', so it gets little probability after other words.

Very large systems have used 'stupid backoff', which multiplies a lower-order score by a constant such as 0.4 and gives scores rather than true probabilities but scales well. Compare perplexities only between models with the same vocabulary.

lessons.title: Hidden Markov models: transitions and emissions
objectives: Describe part-of-speech tagging and common tagsets
Estimate an HMM's transition and emission probabilities from a tagged corpus
key_points: Part-of-speech tagging labels every token with its word class. The Penn Treebank tagset has 45 tags, such as NN, VBD and JJ, while coarse universal tagsets have about a dozen, such as NLTK's 12-tag universal tagset.
Tagging is hard because many common words are ambiguous: 'back' can be a noun, a verb, an adjective, an adverb or a particle, and only the context says which.

A hidden Markov model treats tags as hidden states and words as observations, with transition probabilities P(tag | previous tag), emission probabilities P(word | tag), and a start distribution (transitions from <s>).
It makes two assumptions: each tag depends only on the previous tag (a first-order Markov chain), and each word depends only on its own tag.

Training from a tagged corpus is counting, P(t_i | t_i-1) = count(t_i-1, t_i) / count(t_i-1) and P(w | t) = count(t, w) / count(t), smoothed so unseen pairs aren't impossible. In the Penn Treebank sample, P(NOUN | DET) is 0.637 and P(VERB | DET) only 0.078.

lessons.title: Viterbi decoding
objectives: Explain why the best tag sequence can't be found by trying them all
Decode the best tag sequence with the Viterbi algorithm
key_points: Tagging looks for the tag sequence that maximises P(tags | words), which for an HMM is proportional to the product over positions of P(t_i | t_i-1) × P(w_i | t_i).

Trying every sequence is hopeless, with T^N sequences for T tags and N words, but the Markov assumption means the best path to a tag at one position depends only on the best paths to each tag at the position before.
Viterbi fills a table v[i][t], the probability of the best path ending in tag t at word i: v[i][t] = max over t' of v[i-1][t'] × P(t | t') × P(w_i | t), with the winning t' stored as a backpointer.
At the end it takes the best final tag, including the transition to </s>, and follows the backpointers from right to left to recover the sequence, in time proportional to N × T².

Work in log space, adding log probabilities instead of multiplying, to avoid underflow on long sentences; the same dynamic programme with sums instead of maxima is the forward algorithm, which gives the total probability of the words.

lessons.title: Unknown words and evaluating taggers
objectives: Handle words never seen in training
Evaluate a tagger against a baseline and analyse its errors
key_points: A word never seen in training has emission probability zero under every tag, which wrecks every path through it, and unknown words account for a large share of a tagger's errors.

One fix replaces rare training words, such as those seen once, with shape classes like <-ing>, <-ed>, <CAP> or <NUM>, and maps unseen test words to the same classes, so suffixes and capital letters give clues to the tag.
Morphologically rich languages such as Turkish and Finnish produce far more unseen word forms, so taggers for them lean on morphological analysis or subword features.

Report token accuracy against a baseline that gives each word its most frequent training tag. On the Penn Treebank sample with universal tags that baseline scores 92.6% and the lab's HMM 94.7%: 96.0% on known words but 83.3% on unknown ones.

A confusion matrix of gold against predicted tags shows where a tagger fails: noun-adjective and noun-verb confusions are the commonest, and garden-path sentences such as 'The old man the boats' defeat a bigram HMM.

modules.title: PCFGs and probabilistic parsing
modules.summary: Describe sentence structure with context-free grammars, parse efficiently with the CKY algorithm, choose between ambiguous parses with probabilistic grammars, and see how the inside-outside algorithm learns rule probabilities.

lessons.title: Context-free grammars and constituency
objectives: Write context-free grammar rules for simple English sentences
Explain constituency, parse trees and structural ambiguity
key_points: A constituent is a group of words that behaves as a unit, such as a noun phrase ('the old man') or a prepositional phrase ('with the telescope'): it can be moved, replaced by a pronoun or used alone to answer a question.
A context-free grammar has non-terminal symbols (S, NP, VP), terminal symbols (the words), a start symbol S and rules such as S -> NP VP, each rewriting one non-terminal as a sequence of symbols.

A parse tree shows how the rules derive a sentence from S; treebanks such as the Penn Treebank are corpora of sentences annotated with such trees, written in brackets like (S (NP I) (VP (V saw) ...)).

Structural ambiguity gives one sentence several trees: in 'I saw the man with the telescope' the prepositional phrase can attach to the verb phrase (I used the telescope) or to the noun phrase (the man had it).
nltk.CFG.fromstring() reads a grammar written as text, and parsers such as nltk.ChartParser return every tree the grammar allows, which can be very many for a long sentence.

steps.do: Write a small grammar.
steps.code:
import nltk
cfg = nltk.CFG.fromstring("""
S -> NP VP
NP -> Det N | NP PP | 'I'
VP -> V NP | VP PP
PP -> P NP
Det -> 'the'
N -> 'man' | 'telescope'
V -> 'saw'
P -> 'with'
""")

steps.do: Parse the ambiguous sentence and count the trees.
steps.code:
trees = list(nltk.ChartParser(cfg).parse('I saw the man with the telescope'.split()))
len(trees)

steps.do: Print both trees.
steps.see: One attaches (PP (P with) ...) to the VP; the other puts it inside (NP (NP (Det the) (N man)) (PP ...)).

lessons.title: Chomsky normal form and the CKY algorithm
objectives: Convert a grammar to Chomsky normal form
Recognise and parse sentences with the CKY algorithm
key_points: A grammar in Chomsky normal form (CNF) has only rules of the form A -> B C (two non-terminals) or A -> w (one word); any context-free grammar without empty rules can be converted to an equivalent CNF grammar.

Conversion binarises long rules with new symbols (VP -> V NP PP becomes VP -> V X1 and X1 -> NP PP), replaces words inside longer rules with pre-terminals, and removes unit rules such as NP -> N by copying their expansions upwards.

CKY fills a table whose cell (i, j) holds every non-terminal that can derive words i to j: one-word cells come from the lexical rules, and longer spans combine two adjacent smaller spans with an A -> B C rule, at every split point.
Spans are filled in order of increasing length, so both halves of every split are ready when needed, and the sentence is grammatical if S is in the cell covering all of it.
CKY takes time proportional to n³ times the size of the grammar for n words; backpointers in each cell recover the trees, although an ambiguous sentence can have exponentially many.

lessons.title: Probabilistic CFGs: choosing the best parse
objectives: Compute the probability of a parse tree under a PCFG
Find the most probable parse with probabilistic CKY, and recognise the limits of PCFGs
key_points: A probabilistic CFG gives each rule a probability, and the rules for each left-hand side sum to 1; the probability of a tree is the product of the probabilities of the rules it uses.
Rule probabilities are estimated from a treebank by counting: P(A -> β) = count(A -> β) / count(A).

Probabilistic CKY keeps, in each cell, the highest probability for each non-terminal with a backpointer, so the best tree comes out in the same O(n³) time; NLTK's ViterbiParser does this for nltk.PCFG grammars.

With the lab's toy grammar, the verb-attachment parse of 'I saw the man with the telescope' has probability 0.00040824 and the noun-attachment parse 0.00027216, so the parser prefers the first only because VP -> VP PP (0.3) outweighs NP -> NP PP (0.2).

Plain PCFGs ignore the words when choosing structure, so they misattach phrases whenever the words should decide; lexicalised PCFGs, parent annotation and neural parsers address this. Parsers are scored with labelled precision, recall and F1 over constituents (PARSEVAL).

lessons.title: The inside-outside algorithm, in outline
objectives: Compute a sentence's total probability with the inside algorithm
Describe how inside-outside re-estimates rule probabilities without a treebank
key_points: The inside probability β(A, i, j) is the total probability that A derives words i to j, summed over all its subtrees; it's computed exactly like probabilistic CKY, with sums in place of maxima.
β(S, 0, n) is the probability of the whole sentence, summed over all its parses: 0.00068040 for the lab's ambiguous sentence, of which the best parse holds 60%.
The outside probability α(A, i, j) covers everything outside the span: the probability of generating the words before i and after j with an A filling the gap.
α × β divided by the sentence probability is the expected number of times that constituent appears, and summing these gives the expected count of every rule over a corpus that has no trees.

The inside-outside algorithm is expectation-maximisation: re-estimate rule probabilities from the expected counts and repeat. No round lowers the corpus likelihood, but it can stop at a local maximum, just as the forward-backward algorithm can for HMMs.

files.content:
"""Probabilistic CKY parsing with a small PCFG in Chomsky normal form, checked against NLTK.

Needs only NLTK itself (no data downloads).
"""

import math
from collections import defaultdict

import nltk

GRAMMAR = """
S -> NP VP [1.0]
NP -> Det N [0.6] | NP PP [0.2] | 'I' [0.1] | 'telescopes' [0.1]
VP -> V NP [0.7] | VP PP [0.3]
PP -> P NP [1.0]
Det -> 'the' [0.6] | 'a' [0.4]
N -> 'man' [0.5] | 'dog' [0.2] | 'telescope' [0.3]
V -> 'saw' [1.0]
P -> 'with' [1.0]
"""


def load_rules(text):
    """Binary rules {(B, C): [(A, p)]} and lexical rules {word: [(A, p)]} from a PCFG in CNF."""
    grammar = nltk.PCFG.fromstring(text)
    binary, lexical = defaultdict(list), defaultdict(list)
    for prod in grammar.productions():
        rhs = prod.rhs()
        if len(rhs) == 2:
            binary[(rhs[0].symbol(), rhs[1].symbol())].append((prod.lhs().symbol(), prod.prob()))
        else:
            lexical[rhs[0]].append((prod.lhs().symbol(), prod.prob()))
    return grammar, binary, lexical


def cky(words, binary, lexical):
    """best[(i, j)][A] = (probability, backpointer) of the likeliest A spanning words[i:j]."""
    n = len(words)
    best = defaultdict(dict)
    for i, w in enumerate(words):
        for a, p in lexical.get(w, []):
            best[(i, i + 1)][a] = (p, w)
    # TODO 1: for each span length from 2 to n (shorter spans first), each start i (j = i + length) and each
    #         split point k: for every B in best[(i, k)] and C in best[(k, j)] and every rule A -> B C in
    #         binary[(B, C)], keep A in best[(i, j)] if p(rule) * p(B) * p(C) beats what is there,
    #         storing (probability, (k, B, C)) as its backpointer
    return best


def inside(words, binary, lexical):
    """beta[(i, j)][A] = total probability of all A subtrees over words[i:j]: CKY with sums instead of max."""
    n = len(words)
    beta = defaultdict(lambda: defaultdict(float))
    for i, w in enumerate(words):
        for a, p in lexical.get(w, []):
            beta[(i, i + 1)][a] += p
    # TODO 2: the same loops as cky(), but add p(rule) * beta(B) * beta(C) to beta[(i, j)][A] instead of keeping the max
    return beta


def build_tree(best, i, j, label):
    prob, back = best[(i, j)][label]
    if isinstance(back, str):
        return nltk.Tree(label, [back])
    k, b, c = back
    return nltk.Tree(label, [build_tree(best, i, k, b), build_tree(best, k, j, c)])


def main():
    grammar, binary, lexical = load_rules(GRAMMAR)
    print(f"{len(grammar.productions())} rules, in CNF: {grammar.is_chomsky_normal_form()}")
    words = "I saw the man with the telescope".split()

    best = cky(words, binary, lexical)
    print("Cell (2, 4), 'the man':", {a: round(p, 4) for a, (p, _) in best[(2, 4)].items()})
    print("Cell (1, 7), 'saw ... telescope':", {a: round(p, 6) for a, (p, _) in best[(1, 7)].items()})
    tree = build_tree(best, 0, len(words), "S")
    p_best = best[(0, len(words))]["S"][0]
    print(f"Best parse, p = {p_best:.8f}:")
    print(" ", tree.pformat(margin=200))

    beta = inside(words, binary, lexical)
    total = beta[(0, len(words))]["S"]
    print(f"Inside probability of the sentence: {total:.8f}; the best parse has {p_best / total:.1%} of it")

    parser = nltk.ViterbiParser(grammar)
    nltk_tree = next(parser.parse(words))
    print(f"NLTK ViterbiParser agrees: {nltk_tree.pformat(margin=200) == tree.pformat(margin=200)}, "
          f"p = {nltk_tree.prob():.8f}")
    print(f"Log probability of the best parse: {math.log(p_best):.4f}")
    for sentence in ["the dog saw a man", "the man saw telescopes with the dog", "saw the man"]:
        chart = cky(sentence.split(), binary, lexical)
        s = chart[(0, len(sentence.split()))].get("S")
        print(f"{sentence!r}: {'p = %.6f' % s[0] if s else 'no parse'}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

hints: best[(i, k)] and best[(k, j)] are dicts of {non-terminal: (probability, backpointer)}; the rule's probability multiplies the two child probabilities.
The other parse uses VP -> V NP (0.7) and NP -> NP PP (0.2) where the best one uses VP -> VP PP (0.3) and VP -> V NP (0.7); everything else is shared.
nltk.PCFG.fromstring() raises ValueError ('Productions for NP do not sum to 1') if a left-hand side's probabilities don't add up.

modules.title: Information retrieval foundations
modules.summary: Build the core of a search engine: an inverted index for Boolean queries, ranked retrieval with TF-IDF in the vector space model and with BM25, and the measures that tell you whether the results are any good.

lessons.title: Boolean retrieval and the inverted index
objectives: Build an inverted index of terms and postings lists
Answer Boolean queries by merging postings lists
key_points: An inverted index maps each term to its postings list, the sorted IDs of the documents that contain it, often with the term's frequency and positions; it's built once, so queries never scan the documents.

Documents and queries must go through the same analysis (tokenising, lowercasing, stop-word removal, stemming), or a query for 'ferries' won't match a document saying 'ferry'; the Porter stemmer maps both to 'ferri'.

A Boolean AND intersects postings lists by walking two sorted lists in step and keeping the IDs found in both, in time proportional to their combined length; starting with the rarest term keeps the intermediate results small.
OR merges lists and NOT takes a difference; a positional index, which records where each term occurs, supports phrase queries such as "harbour office".

Boolean retrieval returns an unranked set, exact but brittle: in the lab's collection, 'swimming AND lessons' finds the adult lessons page and misses the school holidays page about children's swimming.

lessons.title: Ranked retrieval: TF-IDF and the vector space model
objectives: Weight terms with TF-IDF
Rank documents by cosine similarity to a query
key_points: Term frequency tf(t, d) counts a term in a document; log scaling, 1 + log10(tf) for tf > 0, stops a term that occurs ten times from counting ten times as much.
Document frequency df(t) counts the documents containing a term, and inverse document frequency idf(t) = log10(N / df(t)) is high for rare, discriminating terms and zero for a term in every document.
A term's TF-IDF weight is its tf weight times its idf. In the lab's 24 documents 'ferri' occurs in 5, so its idf is log10(24/5) ≈ 0.681, while 'swim', in 3, has 0.903.
In the vector space model, documents and queries are vectors of term weights, and documents are ranked by their cosine similarity to the query, which normalises away document length.
Variants are named by their tf, idf and normalisation choices, in SMART notation such as lnc.ltc; whatever you choose, analyse queries and documents the same way.

lessons.title: BM25: a better term weighting
objectives: Explain BM25's term-frequency saturation and length normalisation
Choose and tune BM25's k1 and b parameters
key_points: BM25 scores a document by summing, over the query terms, idf(t) × tf × (k1 + 1) / (tf + k1 × (1 - b + b × dl / avgdl)), where dl is the document's length and avgdl the average length.

The tf part saturates: it rises quickly at first and levels off towards k1 + 1, so the tenth occurrence of a term adds far less than the first; k1, usually between 1.2 and 2.0, sets how quickly it saturates.
b, usually 0.75, controls length normalisation: b = 1 scales tf fully by relative length and b = 0 ignores length, so long documents don't win just by repeating terms.
A common idf for BM25 is ln(1 + (N - df + 0.5) / (df + 0.5)), the form Lucene uses, which stays positive even for terms in most documents.
BM25 has been a strong baseline for decades and is the default ranking in Lucene, Elasticsearch and OpenSearch; on short documents of similar length, like the lab's, it ranks much as TF-IDF does.

lessons.title: Evaluating search: precision, recall, F1 and ranked metrics
objectives: Evaluate retrieval with precision, recall and F1
Score rankings with precision at k and mean average precision
key_points: Evaluation needs a test collection: documents, queries and relevance judgments (qrels) made by people saying which documents are relevant to each query; large collections judge only a pool of the top results from several systems.

For a set of results, precision is the share of retrieved documents that are relevant and recall the share of relevant documents retrieved, and F1 = 2PR / (P + R) balances them; in the lab, 'swimming AND lessons' scores 0.5 on all three.
Precision at k (P@k) looks only at the top k results, which matches what users see, but ignores the order within them and every relevant document further down.

Average precision (AP) averages the precision at each rank where a relevant document appears, counting relevant documents never retrieved as zero; mean average precision (MAP) is its mean over queries.
Other measures weigh other things: reciprocal rank looks only at the first relevant result, and nDCG rewards putting highly relevant documents first when judgments are graded rather than yes or no.

Compare systems on the same queries and judgments, and read individual queries: in the lab, TF-IDF and BM25 both reach a MAP of 0.917, and both rank the train timetable above the storm warning for 'ferry timetable in winter'.

lab.title: Build and evaluate a small search engine

Write a query of your own with relevance judgments, add it to queries.tsv and rerun. Then write two or three sentences starting Evaluation: on what your query and q1 show about matching terms.

d01	Ferry timetable. The ferry to the island leaves the harbour every hour from 7am. In winter the timetable changes and the last ferry leaves at 6pm.
d02	Ferry fares. Single ferry tickets cost 4 euro and returns cost 7 euro. Children travel free on the ferry at weekends.
d03	Storm warnings. When a storm warning is issued, ferry crossings may be cancelled. Check the notice board at the harbour office before you travel.
d04	Station parking. Bicycle parking at the central station is free and covered. Car parking at the station costs 8 euro a day.
d05	Bicycle hire. Hire a bicycle from the kiosk at the station for 10 euro a day. A helmet comes with every bicycle.
d06	Bus routes. Bus route 5 runs from the station to the hospital every 15 minutes. Night buses run on Fridays and Saturdays.
d07	Library opening hours. The central library opens at 9am and closes at 8pm on weekdays. On Sundays the library is closed.
d08	Library cards. Library cards are free for residents. Bring proof of your address to the library desk to join.
d09	Story time. Story time for children runs every Saturday morning in the children's room of the library.
d10	Glass recycling. Glass bottles and jars go in the green recycling bank. Please rinse them and remove the lids.
d11	Recycling collection. Paper, card and plastic recycling is collected every second Tuesday. Put the recycling bin out by 7am.
d12	Garden waste. Garden waste is collected monthly from April to October. Grass and leaves go in the brown bin, not the recycling bin.
d13	Swimming pool. The swimming pool opens at 6am for lane swimming. Swimming lessons for children run on weekday afternoons.
d14	Adult swimming lessons. Swimming lessons for adult beginners run on Tuesday and Thursday evenings at the pool.
d15	Parking permits. Residents can apply for a parking permit online. A permit lets you park on your street without a time limit.

project.title: Integrated POS tagger and text classifier
project.brief: Build a two-stage NLP system and find out honestly whether the first stage helps the second. Train your hidden Markov model tagger, with smoothing, unknown-word classes and Viterbi decoding, on the Penn Treebank sample with universal tags, and report its accuracy on held-out sentences. Then tag every sentence of NLTK's subjectivity dataset (5,000 subjective review snippets and 5,000 objective plot sentences; nltk.download('subjectivity')) and train logistic regression classifiers to tell the two apart with three feature sets: words only, part-of-speech unigrams and bigrams only, and both. Compare them on one stratified test split with accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and confusion matrices, then analyse the errors: which sentences does each model get wrong, and do the tags capture anything the words don't, such as adjectives, first- and second-person pronouns or past-tense narration? In a reference run with an 80/20 split, words alone reached about 91% accuracy, tags alone about 73% and the combination no better than words, so don't assume the tags will help: a clear answer backed by evidence is what earns the marks.
deliverables: tagger.py: the HMM tagger with its accuracy on held-out treebank sentences, overall and for known and unknown words
classify.py: loading and tagging the subjectivity data, the three feature sets, and logistic regression trained and evaluated on one stratified 80/20 split with a fixed seed
A results table of accuracy, precision, recall and F1 for each feature set, with a confusion matrix for each
An error analysis of at least 20 misclassified sentences, grouped by cause, with examples where the tags helped or hurt
A one- to two-page report that answers the question with evidence and says what you'd try next

rubric.name: HMM tagger
rubric.description: Transitions and emissions are estimated with smoothing, unknown words are handled, Viterbi decoding is correct, and accuracy is reported on held-out sentences for known and unknown words.

rubric.name: Features and classifiers
rubric.description: The three feature sets are built correctly from the tagger's output, the classifiers are fitted on the training split only, and every comparison uses the same test split.

rubric.name: Evaluation
rubric.description: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and the confusion matrices are correct and clearly tabulated, with a simple baseline for comparison.

rubric.name: Error analysis
rubric.description: At least 20 errors are examined and grouped by cause with concrete examples, including how tagging mistakes flow into classification mistakes.

rubric.name: Report and code
rubric.description: The report answers the question with evidence and is honest about its limits; the code is organised into functions, runs end to end from one command and fixes its random seeds.
